structure.title: Table of Contents
structure.summary:
# Table of Contents

3.1 Ingestion Layer — Fan-out pipeline, caveats, file types, parsing strategy

3.2 Processing Pipeline — Content Classifier, cross-KB intelligence extraction, chunking

3.3 KB Core — Foundry IQ architecture, structured stores, metadata per KB type

3.4 Product Relationship Graph — Schema, relationship types, 4-layer building, confidence, traversal

3.5 Retrieval Layer — Multi-source query orchestration, per-agent source mapping, query construction

3.6 Cache Layer — What’s cached, TTLs, invalidation strategy

3.7 KB Lifecycle — Update mechanisms, document removal cascade, confidence decay

3.8 Nuances and Risks — Foundry IQ preview status, LLM costs, cold start, quality monitoring

3.9 Key Technical Decisions Summary

structure.title: Module 3: Knowledge Base Engine
structure.prefix_summary:
Module 3 describes the Knowledge Base (KB) Engine, which serves as the intelligence layer of the platform. Its role is to ingest, process, classify, index, and retrieve knowledge that agents use for recommendations, discovery questions, emails, and competitive positioning.

The architecture consists of two parallel systems:

1. **Azure Foundry IQ (managed RAG-as-a-service)** – Handles unstructured content processing, including document parsing, chunking, embedding generation, vector storage, hybrid retrieval (vector + keyword + reranking), query planning, decomposition, and multi-source routing.

2. **Custom KB Layer (built in-house)** – Provides proprietary capabilities such as the Product Relationship Graph, cross-KB content classification and intelligence extraction, structured knowledge stores (e.g., competitor profiles, customer patterns, playbook index), tenant KB lifecycle management, caching, and a Context Assembler that merges all knowledge sources into optimized agent-ready context.

A key architectural distinction is emphasized: the team builds on top of Foundry IQ rather than replacing it. Foundry IQ manages foundational RAG infrastructure, while the custom layer delivers differentiated intelligence, structured knowledge management, and strategic capabilities that form the platform’s competitive advantage.

nodes.title: 3.1 Ingestion Layer
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 3.1 Ingestion Layer

The ingestion layer is a fan-out pipeline. A single file upload triggers multiple parallel downstream processes: raw storage, Foundry IQ indexing, content classification with intelligence extraction, and metadata cataloging. It is not a simple file upload.

nodes.title: 3.1.1 Ingestion Flow — Step by Step
nodes.summary:
This section outlines the end-to-end document ingestion flow for a tenant-isolated knowledge base system.

It begins with uploading files to tenant-scoped blob storage, organized by tenant and category to enforce strict isolation from the outset. The blob storage is configured as a Foundry IQ knowledge source, enabling automatic detection of new files.

Next, the system performs deduplication and versioning by checking a PostgreSQL-based KB catalog. If a file with the same name already exists, it is treated as a new version: the version counter is incremented, the blob URL updated, and re-indexing triggered. If not, a new catalog entry is created. This prevents duplicate records and stale data.

The system then writes a canonical record to the KB catalog in PostgreSQL, storing metadata such as document ID, tenant ID, filename, blob URL, category, version, file type, size, processing status, and upload timestamp. This catalog serves as the source of truth for tenant documents.

An asynchronous background job is triggered to classify the document and extract structured intelligence, running independently from the indexing pipeline.

Finally, Foundry IQ handles automatic indexing: detecting new blobs, parsing, chunking, vectorizing, and indexing them on a scheduled basis or via API trigger. This indexing pipeline is fully managed and not custom-built.

nodes.title: 3.1.2 Ingestion Caveats
nodes.summary:
This section outlines key ingestion caveats in a multi-tenant data processing system.

First, it explains multi-destination routing, where a single uploaded document is simultaneously processed and distributed to multiple system components. For example, one PDF can be stored in raw blob storage, indexed for semantic retrieval, analyzed for product and competitor mentions, used to extract customer outcome data, and recorded in a knowledge base catalog—all from a single upload.

Second, it describes deduplication and versioning requirements. When updated data (such as a revised product catalog) is uploaded, the system must recognize it as a new version of an existing asset rather than a separate item. This triggers version control, re-indexing, and re-execution of analytical processes, including graph analysis and LLM inference.

Third, it emphasizes strict tenant-scoped isolation. All data and metadata must be isolated per tenant from ingestion onward, including storage paths, knowledge bases, and database records. Strong safeguards such as row-level database isolation and separate storage containers are required to prevent cross-tenant data leakage, which would constitute a severe trust breach.

nodes.title: 3.1.3 Supported File Types and Parsing Strategy
nodes.summary:
This section defines the supported file types and the overall parsing strategy for the system, specifying how different document formats are processed, where their data is stored, and why certain architectural decisions were made.

The document distinguishes between structured and unstructured data handling:

For structured data (CSV and Excel product catalogs), a custom parser built with pandas is used. Each row is converted into a product record stored in PostgreSQL, and product descriptions are also sent to Foundry IQ for semantic search. A separate transaction CSV is processed exclusively with a custom parser and used only for building a Product Relationship Graph through co-occurrence and sequential pattern analysis. Transaction data is intentionally not sent to Foundry IQ.

For unstructured documents (PDF, Word, Markdown, PowerPoint, and plain text), parsing is handled entirely by Foundry IQ using Azure Content Understanding. Each format benefits from layout-aware processing:
- PDFs retain table structures, headers as metadata, and figure alt-text.
- Word documents preserve sections and headings.
- Markdown uses header-based chunking with code block preservation.
- PowerPoint processes each slide as a chunk with slide title metadata.
- Plain text is chunked at the paragraph level.

The core architectural decision is to rely on Foundry IQ for all unstructured document parsing and limit custom parsing to structured CSV/Excel files where precise row-level control is required. The rationale is that Foundry IQ provides high-quality, layout-aware enrichment across multiple formats, avoiding the need to build and maintain a complex in-house multi-format parser, which would require significant engineering effort and likely yield inferior results.

nodes.title: 3.2.1 Content Classifier — Cross-KB Intelligence Extraction
nodes.summary:
The partial document describes the **Content Classifier — Cross-KB Intelligence Extraction** system, which serves as the central intelligence extraction layer for uploaded documents. Rather than simply storing documents, the system uses an LLM to analyze and extract structured intelligence that updates multiple downstream knowledge stores simultaneously.

Key points covered:

- **Cross-System Intelligence Updates:** A single uploaded document (e.g., a case study) can automatically update several systems, including:
  - Foundry IQ (semantic indexing)
  - Product Relationship Graph (e.g., detecting cross-sell relationships)
  - Competitor Store (logging competitive mentions and outcomes)
  - Customer Pattern database (capturing outcomes, ROI, metrics)
  - KB Catalog Metadata (tagging products, categories, timestamps)

- **Document Classification Framework:** Documents are categorized into defined types such as product_catalog, case_study, sales_playbook, competitor_intel, pricing_sheet, technical_spec, training_material, and general. Each category has clearly defined intelligence extraction goals.

- **Multi-Category Assignment:** The classifier assigns one primary category and optional secondary categories, enabling documents to serve multiple intelligence functions (e.g., both case study and competitor intel).

- **Structured JSON Extraction:** The LLM returns structured JSON containing detailed extracted intelligence, including:
  - Products mentioned (with SKUs and context)
  - Product relationships (e.g., cross-sell signals)
  - Competitors mentioned and comparison context
  - Customer information (industry, segment, outcomes)
  - Key metrics (revenue impact, timeline, ROI)

- **Model Selection Decision:** The system uses GPT-4.1-mini for classification and structured extraction due to cost efficiency and sufficient performance for schema-constrained tasks, reserving GPT-4.1 for more complex agent interactions. This is particularly important when processing large document batches during onboarding.

Overall, the document outlines an LLM-powered classification and intelligence extraction architecture designed to transform uploaded content into structured, cross-functional business intelligence.

nodes.title: 3.2.2 Intelligence Routing — Fan-Out From Classifier
nodes.summary:
This section describes how extracted intelligence is distributed after a document has been classified. The routing process is designed as independent fan-out steps, meaning failures in one destination do not affect others.

Key points covered:

- **Product Graph Updates:**  
  For each detected product relationship, the system calls `product_graph.add_or_strengthen_edge()` with a medium confidence score sourced from document extraction. If the relationship already exists, it strengthens the edge by adding evidence and increasing the LLM confidence score.

- **Competitor Profile Enrichment:**  
  For each mentioned competitor, the system calls `competitor_store.upsert()` to either create a new competitor profile or enrich an existing one with additional contextual data.

- **Customer Pattern Aggregation:**  
  When customer outcome data is present (e.g., industry, segment, products used, metrics), it is recorded as a success pattern. Multiple case studies for the same industry-segment-product combination are aggregated, increasing the `sample_count` and strengthening the pattern.

- **Knowledge Base Catalog Updates:**  
  The document’s catalog entry is updated to reflect indexing completion. Metadata fields updated include status, primary and secondary categories, mentioned products, full classification metadata (JSON), and a classification timestamp.

Overall, the section outlines a modular, fault-tolerant routing mechanism that distributes classified intelligence into structured systems for products, competitors, customer insights, and catalog metadata.

nodes.title: 3.2.3 Chunking Strategy
nodes.summary:
### Description of Section 3.2.3 – Chunking Strategy

This section explains how document chunking is handled within the system and clarifies ownership responsibilities.

All unstructured document chunking is delegated to **Foundry IQ**. The team configures the behavior but does not build or manage the chunking pipeline. Foundry IQ performs:

- **Semantic text chunking** for standard documents (by paragraphs and sections) with configurable maximum sizes and overlapping windows to preserve context.
- **Layout-aware chunking** (via Azure Content Understanding) for complex documents, ensuring:
  - Tables are extracted as complete units (never split).
  - Headers and section titles are preserved as metadata.
  - Figures include generated alt-text descriptions.
- **Automatic vectorization** of each chunk using the *text-embedding-3-large* model, storing both vectors and raw text to support hybrid retrieval (keyword, vector search, and semantic reranking).

The only custom “chunking” implemented by the team applies to the **product catalog**, which is structured data rather than prose. Each product row is indexed as a standalone structured document (including SKU, name, description, category, price, and features) without further chunking.

The key decision documented is to fully delegate unstructured chunking to Foundry IQ due to the high complexity and engineering effort required to build a robust, layout-aware chunking pipeline. Internal responsibility is limited to transforming product catalog CSV rows into searchable structured documents.

nodes.title: 3.3 KB Core — Knowledge Stores
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 3.3 KB Core — Knowledge Stores

| Two Types of Stores Per Tenant Each tenant has: (1) ONE Foundry IQ Knowledge Base — the unified semantic search layer containing all unstructured content (product descriptions, case studies, playbooks, competitor sheets, technical specs). Not separated into multiple indexes per content type — it is one KB with multiple knowledge sources. (2) FIVE PostgreSQL structured stores — holding queryable structured data: products table, product_relationships (graph), competitor_profiles, customer_patterns, playbook_index, plus the kb_documents catalog. |
| --- |

nodes.title: 3.3.1 Foundry IQ Knowledge Base Architecture
nodes.summary:
This section describes the **Foundry IQ Knowledge Base (KB) Architecture**, focusing on its per-tenant design, retrieval behavior, and configurable reasoning levels.

### Per-Tenant Knowledge Base Structure  
Each tenant has a dedicated knowledge base (`tenant-{tenant_id}-kb`) containing multiple structured knowledge sources stored in tenant-specific blob paths. These sources include:

- Product descriptions  
- Case studies  
- Sales playbooks  
- Competitor intelligence  
- Technical specifications  

### Configuration and Infrastructure  
Key architectural configurations include:

- **LLM Model:** GPT-4.1 used for query planning  
- **Retrieval Reasoning Effort:** Configurable per agent call (low, medium, high)  
- **Indexer Schedule:** Runs hourly in MVP, configurable per tenant in the full product  
- **Semantic Ranker:** Enabled  

### Agentic Retrieval and Query Planning  
When an agent queries the KB, Foundry IQ’s agentic retrieval engine determines which knowledge sources to access. Source routing is handled by the query-planning LLM rather than application code. For example:

- Queries about monitoring solutions may combine product descriptions and case studies.  
- Competitive queries (e.g., against SolarWinds) pull from competitor intelligence.  

### Retrieval Reasoning Levels  
The system supports three configurable reasoning levels:

- **Low:** Basic keyword and vector search without LLM planning. Fast and low-cost; used for quick searches and lightweight plugins.  
- **Medium:** LLM decomposes queries into subqueries with parallel execution and semantic reranking. Used for cross-sell and upsell agents.  
- **High:** Multi-step, iterative reasoning across multiple sources. Highest cost; used for complex, multi-hop solution-building agents.  

Overall, the section outlines a scalable, tenant-isolated knowledge architecture that combines structured content sources with configurable LLM-powered retrieval strategies to support different agent complexity and cost requirements.

nodes.title: 3.3.2 Metadata Model Per KB Type
nodes.summary:
The document section describes a structured metadata model maintained in PostgreSQL to support filtered retrieval and agent-driven workflows across different knowledge base (KB) types. It outlines how enriched metadata complements indexed content to enable precise queries, automation, and decision support.

Key areas covered:

1. **Product Catalog Metadata**  
   Defines structured attributes such as SKU, category, pricing, tier, status, features, target segments, and vendor details. This metadata supports direct SQL lookups, category filtering, and identifying upgrade paths based on product tiers.

2. **Case Study Metadata**  
   Captures customer attributes (industry, segment, size), featured products, pain points, measurable outcomes (ROI, improvement percentages, deal size), sales cycle details, decision-makers, and competitors considered. It enables agents to retrieve relevant case studies based on customer profile and sales context.

3. **Sales Playbook Metadata**  
   Organizes playbooks by workflows (e.g., cross-sell, upsell), product categories, target segments and industries, objections, discovery questions, positioning strategies, and competitive differentiators. This supports selecting the most appropriate playbook for specific sales scenarios.

4. **Competitor Intelligence Metadata**  
   Includes competitor details such as competing SKUs, strengths, weaknesses, win/loss themes, objections, counterarguments, win rates, and deal size metrics. It enables automatic generation of competitor briefs when competitors are mentioned in conversations.

5. **Customer Pattern Metadata**  
   Tracks patterns like successful cross-sells, upgrade journeys, and churn risks, segmented by industry and customer type. It includes deal metrics, sales cycle data, success rates, triggers, blockers, and data sources. This supports predictive insights based on similar customer histories.

Overall, the section explains how structured, queryable metadata across multiple KB types enhances retrieval precision, contextual recommendations, competitive insights, and data-driven sales guidance.

nodes.title: 3.4 Product Relationship Graph
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 3.4 Product Relationship Graph

| Why This Is Our Proprietary Moat Foundry IQ does not know that Product A cross-sells with Product B, that Product C is an upgrade from Product D, or that Products E+F+G form a bundle. This domain-specific knowledge is what makes our recommendations intelligent rather than generic. The Product Relationship Graph is what we build; Foundry IQ cannot replace it. No competitor can replicate a tenant’s graph without their data and usage history. |
| --- |

nodes.title: 3.4.1 Graph Schema
nodes.summary:
This section defines the **Graph Schema** for modeling product-to-product relationships within a multi-tenant system.

It introduces a `product_relationships` table that stores structured connections between two products (`product_a_sku` and `product_b_sku`) under a specific `tenant_id`. Each relationship is categorized by a `relationship_type` (e.g., CROSS_SELL, UPGRADE_PATH, BUNDLE, REPLACES, REQUIRES, COMPETES_WITH) and can be directional to indicate asymmetric relationships (such as upgrade paths).

A key focus is the **multi-source confidence model**, where relationship strength is derived from multiple inputs:
- Statistical co-occurrence data
- LLM-based inference
- Platform usage data
- Administrative review scores  

These inputs are combined into a computed `confidence_composite` score using weighted aggregation. The schema also includes an `evidence` JSONB field to maintain an auditable trail of supporting data.

Additional fields track freshness and update timestamps for statistical data, usage data, and admin reviews. A uniqueness constraint prevents duplicate relationships per tenant and relationship type.

Finally, indexes are defined to optimize graph traversal by product and to enable efficient querying by composite confidence score.

nodes.title: 3.4.2 Relationship Types
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines different types of product relationships used to define how products interact or relate to one another across domains such as IT and insurance. It categorizes relationships by their meaning, directionality (whether the relationship is one-way or bidirectional), and provides practical examples from both industries.

The relationship types include:

- **CROSS_SELL**: Complementary products that are typically sold together, bidirectional in nature.
- **UPGRADE_PATH**: A directional relationship where one product represents a higher-tier version of another.
- **BUNDLE**: Products packaged and sold together as a single offering, non-directional.
- **REPLACES**: A directional relationship where a new product supersedes or replaces an older one.
- **REQUIRES**: A dependency relationship where one product must be present for another to function.
- **COMPETES_WITH**: Products that compete with each other in the market, typically referencing external competitors, and bidirectional.

Overall, the section defines structured product relationship types to standardize how offerings are connected, upgraded, bundled, dependent, replaced, or positioned competitively.

nodes.title: 3.4.3 Four-Layer Graph Building Strategy
nodes.summary:
This section describes a four-layer strategy for automatically building a product relationship graph with minimal human effort, progressively increasing intelligence and confidence.

**Layer 1 – Purchase History Analysis (Zero Customer Effort):**  
Uses uploaded transaction data to detect high-confidence statistical relationships. Techniques include co-occurrence analysis for cross-sell detection, sequential pattern mining for timed cross-sells, upgrade path detection through price/version changes, basket analysis for bundles, and replacement detection when one product substitutes another.

**Layer 2 – LLM Catalog Inference (Zero Additional Effort):**  
Leverages the existing product catalog and applies LLM-based reasoning to infer medium-confidence relationships. It identifies category complementarity, upgrade tiers from naming conventions, feature supersets, price-based tiering, description references, and product replacements based on feature and positioning analysis.

**Layer 3 – Usage Learning (Zero Ongoing Effort):**  
Continuously improves the graph through real-world platform usage. Accepted recommendations, closed deals, recurring customer needs, and sales discovery insights strengthen or create new relationships. Confidence grows over time based on behavioral validation.

**Layer 4 – Human Review (Minimal, Optional, Targeted):**  
Provides admins with a curated review queue of suggested relationships, including confidence scores and evidence. Admins can confirm, edit, reject, or bulk-approve suggestions. The system functions without manual review, but human input enhances accuracy.

Overall, the strategy emphasizes automation first, data-driven confidence building, continuous learning, and optional human validation to refine the product relationship graph efficiently.

nodes.title: 3.4.4 Confidence Model
nodes.summary:
This section describes a **composite confidence scoring model** used to evaluate each graph edge. The overall confidence score is calculated from four weighted sources:

1. **Statistical (35%)** – Based on co-purchase rates from historical data, with a 10% monthly decay if no new co-purchases occur within six months.
2. **LLM Inference (20%)** – Derived from AI-driven catalog analysis, recalculated on catalog updates and not subject to decay.
3. **Usage (30%)** – Based on sales rep acceptance rates and deal close rates, with a 15% monthly decay if no rep acceptance occurs within three months.
4. **Admin (15%)** – Human-reviewed status (confirmed, unreviewed, or rejected), which does not decay over time.

The final score is computed using a weighted formula combining these components and is stored as a generated column in PostgreSQL to optimize query performance.

nodes.title: 3.4.5 Graph Traversal
nodes.summary:
This section describes how agents traverse a product relationship graph using a breadth-first search (BFS) approach starting from a customer’s current product.

It explains an asynchronous function that:
- Traverses product relationships up to a configurable maximum depth.
- Filters relationships by minimum confidence score and optional relationship types.
- Prevents revisiting nodes using a visited set.
- Collects relationship results including source product, target product, relationship type, confidence score, and traversal depth.
- Deduplicates and sorts results before returning them.

The document then outlines how different agents configure traversal parameters based on their purpose:
- Cross-Sell Agent explores CROSS_SELL and BUNDLE relationships up to 2 levels deep.
- Upsell Agent only follows direct UPGRADE_PATH relationships.
- Full Solution Agent performs deeper and broader traversal with lower confidence thresholds.
- Account Overview Plugin limits traversal to direct relationships.
- Background Graph Preloader performs moderate-depth traversal to prepare session data.

Finally, it documents a design decision: using PostgreSQL with an indexed adjacency list for graph storage in the MVP. The rationale is that PostgreSQL is sufficient and performant for expected tenant sizes (50–500 products, 200–2000 edges), while a dedicated graph database like Neo4j would only be considered if graph complexity grows significantly (e.g., over 10,000 edges per tenant or requiring advanced traversal patterns).

nodes.title: 3.5 Retrieval Layer — Multi-Source Query Orchestration
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 3.5 Retrieval Layer — Multi-Source Query Orchestration

When an agent needs knowledge, the Context Assembler (Module 1) calls the KB retrieval layer. This is not a single query — it is a parallel fan-out to multiple sources, with the sources and parameters determined by the agent’s manifest.

nodes.title: 3.5.1 Retrieval Flow
nodes.summary:
This section describes the unified retrieval flow, which performs up to five parallel queries to gather contextual intelligence for the agent.

The process includes:  
1) Foundry IQ semantic retrieval, which builds a contextual query from the conversation state and customer profile, adjusts reasoning effort by agent type, and returns cited text results.  
2) Product Graph traversal, which explores relationships from the customer’s current products to generate product recommendations with confidence scores and supporting evidence.  
3) Competitor Store lookup, triggered when competitors are mentioned, returning structured profiles including strengths, weaknesses, win themes, and counter-arguments.  
4) Customer Patterns query, filtered by industry, segment, and product categories, providing insights such as success rates, average deal sizes, and common triggers or blockers.  
5) Playbook Index query, filtered by workflow type, product categories, and customer segment, returning relevant playbook metadata like discovery questions and objection-handling guidance.

All five queries run concurrently using asynchronous execution, meaning total retrieval time is determined by the slowest query rather than the combined duration of all queries.

nodes.title: 3.5.2 Which Agent Uses Which Sources
nodes.summary:
This section outlines which data sources and knowledge systems each agent or plugin relies on within the platform.

It presents a comparison table mapping agents/plugins to five core data sources: Foundry IQ, Product Graph, Competitor Store, Customer Patterns, and Playbooks.

Key points:

- **Cross-Sell Agent** uses case studies from Foundry IQ, CROSS_SELL and BUNDLE relationships in the Product Graph, relevant customer success patterns, and cross-sell positioning playbooks. It only references competitor data if a competitor is explicitly mentioned.

- **Upsell Agent** relies on case studies and technical specifications from Foundry IQ, UPGRADE_PATH relationships in the Product Graph, upgrade journey patterns, and upsell playbooks. It consults competitor data when competing upgrades exist.

- **Full Solution Agent** uses the most comprehensive set of sources: case studies, technical specs, and playbooks from Foundry IQ; all Product Graph relationship types with deep traversal; the full competitive landscape; and complete customer pattern analysis.

- **Competitor Card Plugin** focuses on competitive intelligence, pulling battle cards from Foundry IQ, COMPETES_WITH edges from the Product Graph, full competitor profiles from the Competitor Store, and win/loss patterns against that competitor. It does not use playbooks.

- **Email Generator Plugin** does not directly query any of these data sources and instead uses existing recommendations.

- **KB Search Plugin** performs direct queries to Foundry IQ based on the sales rep’s search term, without using other systems.

- **Account Overview Plugin** retrieves all Product Graph edges related to a customer’s products and applies matching customer patterns but does not use Foundry IQ, competitor data, or playbooks.

Overall, the section clarifies how each agent or plugin is scoped in terms of data access and analytical depth, ranging from highly specialized (e.g., Email Generator) to fully comprehensive (Full Solution Agent).

nodes.title: 3.5.3 Query Construction for Foundry IQ
nodes.summary:
This section explains how retrieval queries are dynamically constructed for Foundry IQ using structured conversation state rather than the user’s raw message.

The query-building process aggregates multiple contextual elements to improve retrieval relevance:

- **Customer profile information** (industry and market segment) to frame the company context.
- **Existing product categories** to reflect the customer’s current infrastructure.
- **Discovered pain points** identified during the conversation to target specific needs.
- **Agent-specific intent modifiers** based on the active sales strategy (cross-sell, upsell, or full-solution), which adjust the query focus accordingly.

A function (`build_retrieval_query`) assembles these components into a single, enriched natural-language query string. The result is a structured, context-aware query that aligns retrieval results with customer characteristics, existing systems, identified challenges, and the strategic objective of the agent.

nodes.title: 3.6 Cache Layer
nodes.summary:
This section describes the caching strategy used in the system, focusing on performance optimization while maintaining data freshness.

### Key Points Covered

**1. Differentiated Caching Strategy**
Caching is based on data volatility and access patterns. Frequently accessed but relatively stable data is cached in Redis with defined key patterns and time-to-live (TTL) values.

Cached items include:
- **Product graph neighbors (graph traversal results)** – Cached for 6 hours; invalidated when related graph edges are updated.
- **Product details (name, price, features)** – Cached for 24 hours; invalidated when the product catalog is re-uploaded.
- **Competitor profiles** – Cached for 12 hours; invalidated upon competitor intelligence updates.
- **Customer patterns (industry + segment)** – Cached for 24 hours; invalidated during daily pattern recomputation.
- **Preloaded graph context per session** – Stored in session state (Redis) for the lifetime of a user session.

**2. Explicit Decision Not to Cache Foundry IQ Results**
Foundry IQ results are intentionally not cached because:
- Queries are contextual and include evolving conversation state.
- Repeated queries may require different outputs as discovery progresses.
- Caching would risk returning stale results.
- Foundry IQ manages its own internal optimizations.
Caching is therefore limited to slow-changing structured data.

**3. Event-Driven Cache Invalidation**
Cache invalidation is handled through an asynchronous, event-driven mechanism. When knowledge base (KB) content changes, targeted or cascading invalidation occurs:
- Product catalog updates clear product and graph caches and trigger LLM inference reruns.
- Graph edge updates invalidate only affected product graph keys.
- Competitor updates invalidate specific competitor entries.
- Pattern recomputation clears all related pattern caches.

Overall, the section outlines a structured Redis-based caching layer with clearly defined TTLs, key conventions, and precise invalidation logic to ensure consistency, scalability, and freshness of data.

nodes.title: 3.7.1 How Different KB Components Update
nodes.summary:
This section explains how different components of the knowledge base (KB) are updated, including their triggers, mechanisms, and expected latency.

Foundry IQ content updates automatically when an admin uploads or deletes files, triggering incremental reindexing on a scheduled basis (hourly in the MVP), with updates reflected within minutes to hours. The Product Catalog is updated when admins upload new structured files (CSV/Excel); it performs a full re-import with diff detection to show changes before applying them, updating PostgreSQL immediately and reindexing in Foundry IQ within minutes.

The Graph system is divided into four layers. Layer 1 (statistical) recomputes co-occurrence patterns, sequential behaviors, and upgrade detection when new transaction history is uploaded, processed in batch within minutes. Layer 2 (LLM-inferred) reanalyzes the product catalog using LLMs whenever catalog changes occur, also in batch over minutes. Layer 3 (usage-based) updates continuously in real time based on platform usage signals such as rep feedback and deal outcomes. Layer 4 (admin-curated) updates immediately when admins review and confirm or reject suggestions in the Admin Portal.

Competitor Intelligence is refreshed when new competitor documents are uploaded or extracted, triggering classification and data extraction processes that complete within minutes. Customer Patterns are recomputed through scheduled batch jobs (daily or weekly), analyzing transaction data, case studies, and conversations, with processing typically taking hours.

nodes.title: 3.7.2 Document Removal Flow
nodes.summary:
### Description of Document Removal Flow (Section 3.7.2)

This section describes the complete cascade process that occurs when a document is removed from the system. The goal is to ensure that all intelligence, relationships, and derived data sourced from that document are cleanly and safely removed without impacting unrelated data.

Key points covered:

- **Blob Storage Deletion**: The original raw file is removed from the tenant’s blob storage container.

- **Search Index Cleanup (Foundry IQ)**: The system triggers a re-index (automatic or manual), allowing the indexer to detect the missing file and remove its associated chunks from the search index.

- **Graph Data Cleanup**: Any extracted product relationships that reference the document as their evidence source are deleted.

- **Competitor Intelligence Cleanup**: Entries in competitor profiles that were exclusively derived from this document are removed.

- **Customer Pattern Adjustments**: Patterns sourced only from this document are deleted. If a pattern has multiple sources, only this document’s contribution is removed and the sample count is decremented.

- **Soft Deletion in Knowledge Base Catalog**: Instead of hard deletion, the document is marked as deleted (with a timestamp) to preserve an audit trail.

- **Cache Invalidation**: All Redis caches containing data derived from the document are cleared to prevent stale data from being served.

- **Cascade Safety Mechanism**: Every extracted piece of intelligence is tagged with a `source_doc_id`. When a document is removed, the system queries all intelligence linked to that ID and removes or downgrades it accordingly. This ensures precise, surgical cleanup without affecting intelligence derived from other documents.

nodes.title: 3.7.3 Confidence Decay
nodes.summary:
This section explains how confidence scores in product relationship graphs decrease over time to prevent outdated associations from influencing recommendations.

Key points:

- **Purpose of confidence decay:** Product relationships weaken if they are not reinforced, ensuring stale or irrelevant associations do not dominate recommendations.

- **Statistical confidence decay:** If no new co-purchase activity occurs for a product pair within 6 months, its statistical confidence decreases by 10% per month. For example, an 80% confidence score drops significantly over time without reinforcement.

- **Usage confidence decay:** If sales representatives stop accepting recommendations for a product pair for 3 months, usage-based confidence decreases by 15% per month, lowering the priority of relationships that are no longer practically useful.

- **Admin confidence:** Does not decay. Manually set confidence values remain unchanged until explicitly modified by an administrator.

- **LLM confidence:** Does not decay over time but is recalculated whenever the product catalog is updated. If product descriptions still support the relationship, confidence remains.

- **Computation model:** Decay is applied lazily at query time rather than on a scheduled process. When the graph is accessed, the composite confidence score is dynamically adjusted based on the time since each confidence source was last updated.

nodes.title: 3.8 Nuances, Risks, and Design Decisions
nodes.summary:
This section outlines key nuances, risks, and design decisions that impact the MVP architecture and future roadmap.

1. **Use of Preview Features** – Some Foundry IQ capabilities (such as MCP knowledge sources and Azure Content Understanding enrichment) are still in preview as of February 2026. For the MVP, only stable features should be used—specifically blob storage as a knowledge source and basic agentic retrieval with medium reasoning effort. Preview features should not be relied upon for the first tenant deployment.

2. **LLM Classification Cost Considerations** – Each uploaded document triggers an LLM call for classification and intelligence extraction. Large onboarding batches (e.g., 500 documents) can generate hundreds of LLM calls. While costs are manageable using GPT‑4.1‑mini, they must be budgeted. Batch processing with rate limiting is recommended to control spend and avoid API throttling.

3. **Product Graph Cold Start Problem** – New tenants without transaction history can only rely on LLM-based inference (Layer 2), resulting in lower-confidence recommendations. The system still functions, but performs significantly better when transaction data (Layer 1) is available. Tenants should be encouraged to upload historical data to improve recommendation quality.

4. **Future Cross-Tenant Pattern Sharing** – There is potential to leverage anonymized cross-tenant insights (e.g., common cross-sell patterns in insurance), which could enhance recommendations platform-wide. However, this introduces data governance concerns and is explicitly deferred beyond the MVP phase.

5. **Knowledge Base Quality Monitoring** – Ongoing monitoring of each tenant’s knowledge base is critical. Metrics should include document category coverage, document freshness, unused (“dead”) content, and unanswered agent queries. These insights feed into a Knowledge Base health dashboard within the Admin Portal and are essential for customer success and continuous improvement.

nodes.title: 3.9 Key Technical Decisions Summary
nodes.summary:
This section summarizes the core architectural and infrastructure decisions made for the system and explains the rationale behind each choice.

The document first establishes the decision to use Foundry IQ as a managed Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) layer for all unstructured document processing. Instead of building a custom RAG pipeline, the team leverages Microsoft’s managed capabilities (layout-aware enrichment, incremental indexing, semantic reranking) to save engineering time and focus on differentiating components such as the Product Graph, Content Classifier, and structured data stores.

It then defines a multi-tenant knowledge base strategy: one Foundry IQ knowledge base per tenant, shared across all content types. Rather than creating separate knowledge bases for each category, the system relies on Foundry IQ’s agentic retrieval engine to route queries across multiple sources within a single KB, avoiding the need to implement custom source selection logic.

For graph storage, the document specifies using PostgreSQL with an adjacency list model instead of Neo4j for the MVP. Given the expected scale (hundreds of products and thousands of edges per tenant), breadth-first traversal in application code is sufficient. Neo4j is deferred to avoid operational complexity unless future scale or traversal requirements demand it.

A key architectural component is the Content Classifier, positioned as a cross-knowledge-base intelligence hub. Every document is processed by an LLM classifier that extracts structured intelligence and routes it to multiple stores (e.g., Product Graph, Competitor Store, Customer Patterns). This ensures documents contribute structured insights beyond semantic search, creating compounding system-wide intelligence over time.

Finally, the caching strategy is clarified: only structured data (e.g., graph traversals, product details, competitor profiles) is cached in Redis, while Foundry IQ query results are not cached. Since Foundry IQ responses are highly contextual and conversation-dependent, caching them risks stale outputs, whereas structured data changes infrequently and benefits significantly from caching.
